## Introduction

Every process on a GPU shares its memory: your R session, other R sessions, a
Python notebook, the desktop. cuplyr allocates many short-lived columns while
it runs a pipeline. How it asks the driver for that memory decides how fast
each call is, how much of the card cuplyr keeps after you drop a table, and how
much is left for other processes.

This article covers the three ways cuplyr can allocate, how to switch between
them, how to read what cuplyr holds, when memory is freed, and how to choose.
It ends with numbers from one machine.

```{r setup}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

## The three resources

When it loads, cuplyr installs one RMM memory resource. Every GPU allocation in
the R process goes through it.

| Resource | What it is | Speed per allocation | Memory after you drop a table | Sharing the card |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"async"` (default) | CUDA's stream-ordered allocator (`cudaMallocAsync`) | Fast, same as the pool | Cached for reuse until `gpu_gc()` returns it, or returned by CUDA with the opt-in `cuplyr.release_threshold` | Good, `gpu_gc()` hands back what you dropped |
| `"pool"` | RMM's pool, one big reservation split into columns | Fast | Kept until the R session ends, the pool never shrinks | Poor, the card stays as full as your peak |
| `"cuda"` | No resource, a plain `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` per column | Slowest | Returned to the device when R collects the table | Good, but every allocation pays the driver |

With `async`, cuplyr reserves `cuplyr.pool_initial` bytes at load so the first
calls need no driver allocation. The default is a quarter of free device
memory, at most 1 GiB. The async pool then grows when a pipeline needs more and
keeps what it grew to for the next call, which is why it is as fast as the
pool. Unlike the pool it can give memory back. `gpu_gc()` synchronises the
device and returns everything the async pool holds unused, so a pipeline that
briefly needed 6 GB doesn't hold 6 GB for the rest of the session.

### Automatic release

To get memory back without calling `gpu_gc()`, set `cuplyr.release_threshold`
in bytes. At every GPU synchronisation, CUDA then returns unused memory until
the pool's whole reservation is at or below the threshold. The reservation
includes the tables you hold and results R hasn't collected yet. So while your
session holds more than the threshold, nothing freed stays cached, and every
allocation goes to the driver at about the speed of plain `cudaMalloc`. A
threshold of `0` keeps nothing. libcudf synchronises inside many calls, not
only in `collect()`, `print()` and `gpu_sync()`, so a release can happen in the
middle of a pipeline. The table at the end shows the cost.

## Switching resources

cuplyr picks the resource when the package loads, one per R process. Set the
option before `library(cuplyr)`, and restart R to change it.

| What | Option | Environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| Kind of resource: `"async"` (default), `"pool"`, or `"cuda"`/`"none"` for no resource | `cuplyr.memory_resource` | `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE` |
| Turn the resource off (`"cuda"`): `FALSE`, `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"`, `"off"` | `cuplyr.memory_pool` | `CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL` |
| How much the resource reserves at load, in bytes (not a limit) | `cuplyr.pool_initial` | `CUPLYR_POOL_INITIAL` |
| Async only: release unused memory automatically while the whole reservation is above this many bytes | `cuplyr.release_threshold` | `CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD` |

An option wins over its environment variable. Case and surrounding spaces
don't matter. `cuplyr_options()` shows the values as set now, which take effect
at the next load, not the ones this session's resource was installed with.
`?"cuplyr-options"` documents them all.

cuplyr warns about invalid values and falls back:

- An unknown kind, say `"managed"`, gives `"async"`. If `cuplyr.memory_pool`
  turns the resource off, the kind is ignored and no resource is used.
- A `cuplyr.release_threshold` of `NA` or `""` counts as unset, so the
  environment variable decides. Any other value that isn't a non-negative
  number means no automatic release. `"pool"` and `"cuda"` ignore the
  threshold.
- If the GPU or driver doesn't support `cudaMallocAsync` and async was only the
  default, cuplyr installs `"pool"`. If you asked for `"async"` by name, it
  installs no resource (`"cuda"`).

```{r switch, eval = FALSE}
# In a fresh R session, before loading cuplyr:
options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "pool")   # the pool instead of async
# or: options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "cuda")  # plain cudaMalloc; same as
#     options(cuplyr.memory_pool = FALSE)
# or: options(cuplyr.release_threshold = 0)      # async: keep nothing cached
library(cuplyr)
```

From a shell, `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool Rscript script.R` does the same.
`cuplyr.pool_initial = 0` only skips the reservation at load. The pool still
grows and caches as it needs.

## Reading the numbers

`gpu_memory_state()` reports the device and what cuplyr's resource holds.

```{r state}
st <- gpu_memory_state()
st$resource
c(free = st$free_bytes, pool = st$pool_bytes, in_use = st$pool_used_bytes)
```

* `free_bytes`, `used_bytes` and `total_bytes` cover the whole device, every
  process, as `nvidia-smi` shows. `used_bytes` includes memory the resource
  keeps for reuse, so dropping a table doesn't lower it until the memory goes
  back. Under `"pool"` that never happens. Under `"async"` it happens after
  `gpu_gc()` or an automatic release.
* `pool_bytes` is what cuplyr's resource holds from the device.
* `pool_used_bytes` is what cuplyr uses for live columns and scratch space. It
  rises when you create a table and falls when R collects it.
* Under `"cuda"` there is no resource, so `pool_bytes` and `pool_used_bytes` are
  `NA` and `free_bytes` tells the whole story.

To see how big your tables are, read `pool_used_bytes`. To see how much of the
card you take from others, read `pool_bytes` or `free_bytes`.

```{r usage}
gpu_df <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1e6)), lazy = FALSE)
gpu_memory_usage(gpu_df)  # estimate from dimensions and types
gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
```

`gpu_memory_usage()` estimates a table's size from its row count and column
types without touching the device. Tables that share columns, such as a
`select()` of another table, overlap in this estimate.

## When is memory freed?

1. A call frees its own intermediates. A lazy table, the default, holds nothing
   for its pending steps. An eager verb, `compute()`, `collect()` or
   `bind_rows()` frees the temporary tables its steps built when it returns.
2. Tables you hold live until R's garbage collector runs. After `rm(gpu_df)`
   the memory is freed when R collects it. R doesn't know about GPU memory
   pressure, so that can be late.
3. `gpu_gc()` forces the collection. Under `async` it then returns all unused
   memory to the device. The next calls must grow the pool again, which costs
   the first call a few percent, so keep it out of timing loops. In the list it
   returns, `freed_bytes` is the drop in `pool_used_bytes` and `released_bytes`
   the drop in `pool_bytes`. `released_bytes` is 0 under `"pool"` and `NA`
   under `"cuda"`. If the device is in a CUDA error state, `gpu_gc()` warns
   instead of failing.
4. When a GPU step runs out of device memory, cuplyr runs `gc()` and
   `gpu_gc(aggressive = FALSE)` and retries the step once. A second failure
   raises an error of class `cuplyr_error_gpu_oom`.

```{r gc}
rm(gpu_df)
res <- gpu_gc()
c(freed = res$freed_bytes, released = res$released_bytes)
```

## How to choose

* Keep the default, `async`, unless you have a reason not to. It is as fast as
  the pool and `gpu_gc()` hands its memory back.
* Use `"pool"` only when cuplyr is the card's only user. It never gives memory
  back, not even after `gpu_gc()`. Released cuplyr versions up to 0.1.1 used
  no resource, which is `"cuda"`.
* Use `"cuda"` to debug memory, since device free memory is then exactly what
  you hold. Calls are slower.
* If you share the card, stay on `async` and call `gpu_gc()` after a large job.
  If you can't, set `cuplyr.release_threshold` above what your session holds
  while it works, counting live tables and uncollected results. Below that,
  every call allocates from the driver and runs at about the speed of `"cuda"`.
* No resource lets data bigger than the card fit. They only change how much is
  held on the side.

## Measured on this machine

Measured on 2026-10-23 with cuplyr 0.1.1.9000 on an RTX 5070 (12 GB). Each
number is the median of 3 fresh R processes per configuration. The table is
static and nothing is timed when this vignette builds.

The columns are `async` as shipped, `async` with `cuplyr.release_threshold = 0`,
`pool`, and `cuda`. Per-call time is the median over batches of calls after
warm-up, with a GPU synchronisation at the end of each batch.

* Small eager mutate: `mutate(z = x * 2 + y)` on an eager 1000-row table.
* 1e6-row lazy pipeline: `filter()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`, `summarise()`
  and `collect()` on a lazy 1e6-row table.
* 25M-row workflow: the README benchmark (`filter()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`,
  `summarise()`, `collect()`) on a lazy table of 25 million rows and 6 columns,
  about 1 GB on the GPU.

Held memory is extra device memory in use compared with a starting point taken
after `gpu_gc()` and before the table exists. "After gc + sync" means after
dropping the table, running `gc()` and synchronising. The last row is
`pool_bytes` after the 1 GB run's `gpu_gc()`.

| Measurement | `async` | `async`, `release_threshold = 0` | `pool` | `cuda` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small eager mutate (ms per call) | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.84 | 0.87 |
| 1e6-row lazy pipeline (ms per call) | 3.3 | 3.5 | 3.3 | 4.1 |
| 25M-row workflow (ms per call) | 14.3 | 19.0 | 14.3 | 18.0 |
| 1 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) | 1.01 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 1 GB table, after `gpu_gc()` (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 3 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) | 3.02 | 0.00 | 4.29 | 0.00 |
| 3 GB table, after `gpu_gc()` (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.29 | 0.00 |
| Held by the resource after `gpu_gc()`, 1 GB run (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.29 | n/a (no resource) |

* Default `async` and `pool` run at the same speed. Plain `cuda` is slower at
  1e6 rows (4.1 ms) and about 25% slower on the 25M-row workflow (18.0 ms).
* `async` with `release_threshold = 0` keeps nothing after a synchronisation,
  but every call allocates from the driver again. The 25M-row workflow takes
  19.0 ms, about a third slower than the default.
* Default `async` keeps a dropped table cached (1.01 and 3.02 GB) until
  `gpu_gc()` returns all of it.
* `pool` ran its measurements in order in one process, and the 25M-row workflow
  had already grown the pool to 4.29 GB. The 1 GB table fit inside that. The
  3 GB table grew the pool by another 4.29 GB, since it grows in large steps,
  and the pool kept it even after `gpu_gc()`.
* `cuda` gets memory back as soon as R collects the table.

To repeat the measurement, run the code below once per configuration, each in a
fresh session started with `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async`,
`CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD=0`,
`CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool`, or `CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL=0`, and take the median of
a few runs.

```{r measure, eval = FALSE}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)

# Median seconds per call over `samples` batches of `reps` calls.
per_call <- function(fn, reps, samples = 15, warmup = 5) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync()
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  median(t)
}

small <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1000), y = runif(1000)), lazy = FALSE)
1e3 * per_call(function() mutate(small, z = x * 2 + y), reps = 200)

big <- data.frame(x = runif(1e6), y = runif(1e6), k = sample.int(100L, 1e6, TRUE))
lz <- tbl_gpu(big, lazy = TRUE)
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  lz |> filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y) |>
    group_by(k) |> summarise(s = sum(z)) |> collect()
}, reps = 10)
rm(small, lz, big)

# README-scale workflow: 25M rows x 6 columns (about 1 GB on the GPU).
n <- 25e6
taxi <- data.frame(
  VendorID = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  payment_type = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE),
  fare_amount = pmax(2.5, rnorm(n, mean = 13, sd = 10)),
  tip_amount = pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 2.5, sd = 3)),
  tolls_amount = runif(n, 0, 15),
  trip_distance = pmax(0.1, rexp(n, rate = 0.3)))
tg <- tbl_gpu(taxi, lazy = TRUE)
rm(taxi); gc()
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  tg |> filter(fare_amount > 0, trip_distance > 0) |>
    mutate(fare_per_mile = fare_amount / trip_distance) |>
    group_by(VendorID, payment_type) |>
    summarise(avg_fare_per_mile = mean(fare_per_mile),
              avg_tip = mean(tip_amount), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect()
}, reps = 3, samples = 9, warmup = 2)
rm(tg)

# Held memory for a table of n doubles (1.25e8 = 1 GB, 3.75e8 = 3 GB).
held <- function(n) {
  host <- data.frame(a = runif(n))
  gpu_gc()
  free0 <- gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes   # the starting point
  g <- tbl_gpu(host, lazy = FALSE)
  gpu_sync()
  rm(g); gc(); gc()
  gpu_sync()
  after_gc_sync <- free0 - gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes
  gpu_gc()
  s <- gpu_memory_state()
  after_gpu_gc <- free0 - s$free_bytes
  c(after_gc_sync = after_gc_sync, after_gpu_gc = after_gpu_gc,
    pool_bytes = s$pool_bytes) / 1e9
}
held(1.25e8)
held(3.75e8)
```
